title: Area I review: Preflight Preparation
intro: These questions mix the eight taught Tasks of Area I: pilot qualifications, airworthiness, weather, cross-country planning, the airspace system, performance, airplane systems and human factors. Many join two of them in one real commercial preflight, the way an examiner would ask.

questions.q: You were 42 when you passed a second-class medical exam in August 2025. Today is October 22, 2026, and you have no newer medical. Which is true?
options: You may still fly paid charters, because a second-class medical lasts 24 months after age 40
You may not use commercial privileges, but the medical still covers private pilot privileges through August 31, 2027
You may not act as PIC at all until you get a new medical
You may fly paid flights under BasicMed until you see an AME
questions.why: For commercial privileges a second-class medical expires at the end of the last day of the 12th month after the exam month, at any age, so it ran out on August 31, 2026 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]]. For private privileges, if you were 40 or older at the exam, it lasts to the end of the 24th month: August 31, 2027 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(iii)]]. The 24-month figure belongs to private privileges, not commercial ones. BasicMed never covers commercial privileges, which need a first- or second-class medical [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]].

questions.q: You plan an IFR trip through a stratus layer with tops near 11,000 ft. The FB reads 2415+05 at 6,000 ft and 2520-01 at 9,000 ft. Your airplane has pitot heat and an alternate static source and is not certificated for icing. Which altitude plan is best?
options: 9,000 ft, since the freezing level is where the FB first shows a minus sign
12,000 ft, climbing quickly through the layer to the tops
10,000 ft with pitot heat on, since the airplane has ice protection
About 8,000 ft or lower, below a freezing level near 8,500 ft
questions.why: FB temperatures are the last two digits, in °C [[28:405|AWH 27-4]], and the freezing level can be found from the winds aloft forecast [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1g]]. From +05 to -01 is 6 °C in 3,000 ft, or 2 °C per 1,000 ft, so 0 °C is 5 / 2 x 1,000 = 2,500 ft above 6,000 ft: about 8,500 ft. At 8,000 ft it is about +1 °C. Expect icing in any cloud at or below 0 °C [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]]. Nearly all airplanes have pitot heat and alternate static, and that does not make one icing-certificated; an airplane not certified for icing must avoid it [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13]]. Climbing to 12,000 ft means about 2,500 ft of below-freezing cloud on the way up, and 9,000 ft is already at -1 °C.

questions.q: You fly sightseeing passengers for an operator that holds a 91.147 Letter of Authorization. The airplane's last 100-hour inspection was at 2,410.0 hours time in service, and it is now at 2,503.6. Each tour adds 0.5 hour of time in service. How many more tours may you fly before the inspection?
options: As many as you like, since the 100-hour rule covers only flight instruction
questions.why: A 91.147 operator carries passengers for compensation or hire [[60:463|14 CFR 91.147(a)]], and carrying any person other than a crewmember for hire needs an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Time in service runs from leaving the surface to touching down at the next landing [[60:16|14 CFR 1.1]]. The inspection is due at 2,410.0 + 100 = 2,510.0, so 2,510.0 - 2,503.6 = 6.4 hours remain. 12 tours use 6.0 hours; a 13th would end at 2,510.1, over the limit. 32 comes from adding the 10-hour allowance, but that time is only for flying en route to a place where the inspection can be done [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]], not for more paid tours.

questions.q: Surface temperature 24 °C, dewpoint 14 °C, at a field 1,000 ft MSL on flat ground. You plan a VFR leg on a magnetic course of 095° in Class E airspace, under the cumulus that will form. Which cruise plan meets both the cloud clearance and the cruising altitude rules?
options: 5,500 ft MSL, the eastbound altitude just above the cloud bases
4,500 ft MSL, 500 ft below the bases
3,500 ft MSL, below 3,000 ft AGL, where the cruising altitude rule does not apply
6,500 ft MSL, on top of the cumulus
questions.why: Bases are about spread / 2.5 x 1,000 = 10 / 2.5 x 1,000 = 4,000 ft AGL, so about 5,000 ft MSL here [[28:146|AWH 12-2]]. In Class E below 10,000 ft MSL you must stay 500 ft below clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]], so 4,500 ft MSL is the highest you can go. The cruising altitude rule applies only in level cruise more than 3,000 ft above the surface, and on 095° asks for odd thousands plus 500 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]]. 4,500 ft MSL is 3,500 ft AGL, so it would need an odd altitude, and 5,500 ft is in the bases. 3,500 ft MSL is 2,500 ft AGL, where the rule does not apply, and it keeps 1,500 ft below the clouds. 6,500 ft is a westbound altitude. Application: bases from the spread are an estimate, so check reports in flight.

questions.q: A school offers you an airplane with retractable gear, flaps, a constant-speed propeller, a 200-horsepower engine and round gauges. You have flown only fixed-gear trainers. What do you need before you act as its PIC?
options: Only a high-performance endorsement, because of the 200-horsepower engine
No endorsement, because the time counts toward your 10 hours of advanced-airplane training
Logged ground and flight training and a one-time complex endorsement
Logged training plus both complex and high-performance endorsements
questions.why: Retractable gear, flaps and a controllable-pitch propeller make it a complex airplane [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]], so you need logged ground and flight training and a one-time endorsement [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(e)]]. High-performance means an engine of more than 200 horsepower [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]], and exactly 200 is not more than 200. With round gauges it is not a TAA either [[60:321|14 CFR 61.129(j)]]. Whether the time counts toward 61.129 is a separate question from the 61.31 endorsement. Expect new gear errors, like forgetting to extend it, and fly the checklist every time [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

questions.q: You will land in 30 minutes. The destination METAR issued at 1853Z ends RMK AO2 PK WND 31038/34 WSHFT 20 FROPA PRESRR. What does it tell you?
options: A front passed at 1820Z; expect gusty, turbulent wind behind it, with a peak wind since the last report of 38 kt from 310°
The peak wind was 38 kt from 340° at 1834Z, and the pressure is steady
Wind shear of 20 kt is forecast with the front
A cold front is still approaching; expect a wind shift soon and falling pressure
questions.why: PK WND 31038/34 is a peak wind of 38 kt from 310° at 34 minutes past the hour [[28:304|AWH 24-20]]. WSHFT 20 FROPA is a wind shift that began at 20 past the hour, likely from a frontal passage [[28:305|AWH 24-21]]. PRESRR means pressure rising rapidly [[28:308|AWH 24-24]]. Pressure falls ahead of a cold front, bottoms out at passage and then rises, and behind a fast-moving cold front skies usually clear but gusty, turbulent winds remain [[28:139|AWH 11-6]]. So the front is past, not coming. The 20 in WSHFT is a time, not a wind shear value.

questions.q: You load the W&B Handbook sample airplane (max takeoff 3,100 lb, max landing 2,950 lb) to 3,040 lb, with 40 gallons of fuel, for a 45-minute leg at 12 GPH plus 3 gallons for start, taxi and climb. What should you do?
options: Plan to circle and burn 15 gallons before landing, since you will be 90 lb over
Nothing; the landing chart is entered with the takeoff weight, which is legal
Nothing; the takeoff weight is under 3,100 lb
Take off at least 18 lb lighter, for example 3 gallons less fuel, so you land at or below 2,950 lb
questions.why: Planned burn: 45 / 60 x 12 = 9 gallons, plus 3 = 12 gallons, x 6 lb per gallon = 72 lb [[22:67|W&B Handbook 7-7]]. Landing weight: 3,040 - 72 = 2,968 lb, which is 18 lb over the 2,950 lb maximum [[22:50|W&B Handbook 5-2]]. 18 lb / 6 = 3 gallons. With 37 gallons you still carry far more than the 12 gallons of trip fuel plus 6 gallons of day reserve (30 minutes at 12 GPH) [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]]. The 90 lb figure forgets the fuel you burn on the way. Landing distance is worked with landing weight, not takeoff weight [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]]. A quick return for a problem would land even heavier, so fix the load on the ground.

questions.q: At 1900 tonight your doctor starts you on a new prescription medicine for a new condition. You are booked as PIC of a charter at 0800 tomorrow. What is the best decision?
options: Fly if you feel fine at 0700, since 12 hours will have passed
Hand the trip to another pilot, wait at least 48 hours after the first dose, and ask an AME whether the condition or medicine is disqualifying
Fly, but take a second pilot along as a safety pilot
Fly; 91.17 covers only alcohol and illegal drugs
questions.why: The PHAK says to wait at least 48 hours after the first dose of any new medicine, OTC or prescribed, to see whether it has side effects that make flying unsafe [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. 91.17 bans crew duty while using any drug that affects your faculties in any way contrary to safety, not just alcohol [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. You also may not act as PIC while you know of a condition, or take medication for it, that would make you fail the medical you need [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]], which is second class for commercial privileges [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]]. The condition itself may be disqualifying even when the drug is fine [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. A second pilot does not fix an impaired PIC.

questions.q: True course 183°, variation 5° E, and the wind calls for a 4° right correction. You will cruise VFR more than 3,000 ft AGL. Which altitudes fit?
options: Odd thousands plus 500, because the magnetic course is 178°
Either one, since you may use course or heading
Even thousands plus 500, because the magnetic heading is 182°
Even thousands plus 500, because the true course is 183°
questions.why: East variation is subtracted [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]]: magnetic course 183 - 5 = 178°. The cruising altitude rule uses magnetic course, and 0° to 179° calls for odd thousands plus 500 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]]. The magnetic heading, 183 + 4 - 5 = 182°, includes the wind correction, and the rule does not use heading. True course skips the variation.

questions.q: Westbound VFR at 12,500 ft MSL over terrain near 9,000 ft MSL, in Class E airspace in the 48 states, you will cruise for 90 minutes in an unpressurized airplane under Part 91. Which statement is correct?
options: The required crew must use oxygen for the 60 minutes beyond the first 30
You need 3 SM visibility and 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft from clouds
You need Mode C and ADS-B Out, and 5 SM visibility with 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM from clouds; 91.211 does not require oxygen at this altitude
No transponder is needed, because you are more than 2,500 ft above the ground
questions.why: At and above 10,000 ft MSL over the 48 states, Mode C and ADS-B Out are required except at and below 2,500 ft above the surface. You are 3,500 ft above it, so both apply [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]]. In Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL the minimums are 5 SM, 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. The 30-minute oxygen rule starts above 12,500 ft cabin altitude, so at 12,500 ft it does not apply [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]]. The AIM still encourages oxygen above 10,000 ft by day [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]], which is wise on a 90-minute leg.

questions.q: A NOTAM closes the longest runway at your destination for your ETA. The other runway is 3,100 ft, smooth (not grooved), and reported wet with good braking (RwyCC 5). Your piston airplane's unfactored dry AFM landing distance is 1,250 ft. Using AC 91-79B, what do you decide?
options: Land; 1,250 ft is less than half the runway
Land; with the dry factor of 1.67 you need about 2,088 ft
Land; with the factor of 2.3 you need about 2,875 ft
Plan another airport; with the factor of 2.6 you need about 3,250 ft
questions.why: For any flight you must know the runway lengths and AFM landing distance data at the airports you will use [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]], and runway closures come by NOTAM [[33:327|AIM TBL 5-1-1]]. For a reciprocating airplane, the AC 91-79B factor for good braking on a smooth runway is 2.6: 1,250 x 2.6 = 3,250 ft, more than the 3,100 ft you have [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. The 2.3 factor is for a grooved or PFC runway, and 1.67 is for dry. The factors already include a 15 percent safety margin [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3-2]], so there is nothing to shave off.

questions.q: Forty minutes from your destination, the ammeter shows a full-scale discharge and the alternator light comes on. A towered airport is 12 minutes to your left. Your gear and flaps are electric. What is the best plan?
options: Keep all equipment on so ATC can see you, and lower the gear and flaps electrically as usual
Shed nonessential loads, turn toward the nearer airport now, tell ATC, and plan a manual gear extension and a no-flap landing
Continue to the destination, since a 25 amp-hour battery gives 5 hours
Turn toward the nearer airport, but only after working out the new heading, groundspeed and fuel
questions.why: A full-scale minus reading points to the alternator [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]. The battery then may not last long: 5 hours at 5 amps, about 2 hours at 10 amps, and 10 to 15 minutes at 40 amps [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Shed non-essential loads at once and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Tell ATC, and with electric gear and flaps expect a no-flap landing and a manual gear extension [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. In an emergency, divert promptly; doing all the computations first can make it worse, so work out the new numbers once you are established on course [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].

questions.q: The airplane's transponder was last tested and inspected on September 12, 2024. Today is October 22, 2026, and your VFR route crosses Class C airspace. What is true?
options: It is fine; the test is good for 24 calendar months, through September 30, 2027
It is fine; the 24-month test applies only to flights under IFR
The test ran out at the end of September 2026, so you may not use the transponder; route outside airspace that requires one, or get it tested first
The transponder needs a test every 12 calendar months, so it ran out in 2025
questions.why: No one may use a transponder unless it was tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]]. Calendar months run to the last day of the month [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]], so a September 2024 test lasts through September 30, 2026. Class C requires a Mode C transponder [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(1)]]. The test that applies only to IFR in controlled airspace is the altimeter, static and encoder check [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]]. You cannot do the transponder test yourself; a rated repair station does it [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(c)]].

questions.q: On a Part 135 on-demand charter in an unpressurized airplane, you cruise at 11,500 ft MSL for 50 minutes. What oxygen must you, the pilot, use?
options: Oxygen for 20 minutes, the part of the time at that altitude beyond 30 minutes
Oxygen for the whole 50 minutes
None for you, but every passenger must be provided oxygen
None, since 91.211 starts at cabin altitudes above 12,500 ft
questions.why: Part 135 is stricter than Part 91. Each pilot of an unpressurized aircraft uses oxygen above 10,000 ft through 12,000 ft MSL for the part of the flight at those altitudes over 30 minutes, and continuously above 12,000 ft [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89(a)]]. 50 - 30 = 20 minutes. Under Part 91 alone nothing would be required until above 12,500 ft, and passengers must be provided oxygen only above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. Your commercial privileges always depend on the rules of the operation you fly in [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]].

questions.q: At 0545 you start planning a paid photo flight that departs at 0900. Which briefing plan follows the guidance?
options: An outlook briefing now, because departure is more than 2 hours away
A standard briefing now, asking for current conditions, then an abbreviated briefing to update it just before departure
An abbreviated briefing now and a standard briefing right before departure
A standard briefing now; it always includes current conditions, so nothing more is needed
questions.why: Departure is 3 hours 15 minutes away. An outlook briefing is for a departure 6 or more hours away, a standard briefing is for within 6 hours of flight, and an abbreviated briefing updates a standard one as soon as practical before flight [[37:8|AC 91-92 Table 1]]. When departure is more than two hours away, a standard briefing leaves out current conditions unless you ask for them [[28:27|AWH 3-4]]. So the 2-hour point changes what the standard briefing includes, not which briefing you get.

questions.q: The bottom of your airspeed indicator's green arc is 60 knots, and you are at max takeoff weight. To avoid a building cumulus close ahead, you roll into a coordinated level turn at 60° of bank. About what speed will the airplane now stall at?
options: 120 knots
70 knots
60 knots
85 knots
questions.why: The bottom of the green arc is VS1, the clean stall speed at max takeoff weight [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. A level 60° turn is 2 Gs in any airplane [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], and stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]: 60 x 1.414 = 84.9, about 85 knots. 120 knots doubles the speed instead of using the square root. 70 knots is the AFH example for an airplane that stalls at 50 knots, not this one.

questions.q: Thirty minutes before sunset, a Class D airport reports 2 SM in mist with an overcast ceiling at 700 ft, temperature 9 °C and dewpoint 8 °C. You hold a commercial ASEL certificate without an instrument rating. What does a legal departure require?
options: A special VFR clearance, clear of clouds, at least 1 SM visibility, and the SVFR part finished before sunset
A special VFR clearance, which also gives you ATC separation for the whole trip
A special VFR clearance; commercial pilots may use it after sunset, so the time does not matter
Nothing extra; 2 SM is enough to depart VFR from Class D
questions.why: Under basic VFR you may not fly beneath a ceiling below 1,000 ft, or take off without 3 SM, inside the surface area [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)-(d)]]. Special VFR needs an ATC clearance, clear of clouds, 1 SM flight visibility and 1 SM ground visibility for takeoff, and it is allowed between sunset and sunrise only for a pilot who meets the instrument requirements, in an IFR-equipped airplane [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)-(c)]]. The clearance and the separation work only inside the surface area [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. With a 1 °C spread at dusk, expect the weather to get worse: fog seldom forms when the spread is more than 2 °C [[28:222|AWH 18-2]], and here it is well under that.

questions.q: In cloud at -3 °C, your fuel-injected engine with a constant-speed propeller slowly loses manifold pressure, from 24 to 20 inches, while the rpm stays steady. What is most likely, and what do you do?
options: Detonation; reduce power and enrich the mixture
Governor failure; pull the propeller control back
Impact ice blocking the air intake or filter; select alternate air and get out of the icing
Carburetor ice; apply full carburetor heat
questions.why: With a constant-speed propeller the governor holds rpm, so induction icing or a clogged air filter shows as a loss of manifold pressure, and the generic fix is alternate air [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]. Fuel injection is less prone to icing, but impact ice can still block the air intake [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]], and the alternate air source lets air bypass a clogged filter [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]. A fuel-injected engine has no carburetor to ice. Detonation shows as high cylinder head temperature, and governor trouble as surging rpm [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]. You are in cloud below 0 °C, so expect airframe ice as well [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]].

questions.q: A military jet intercepts you near a TFR. After you follow it for a while, it makes an abrupt climbing turn of more than 90° away from you, without crossing your path. What does it mean, and how do you answer?
options: You have been intercepted, follow me; rock your wings and follow
Leave the area at once; squawk 7600
Land at this airport; lower the gear and follow
You may proceed; rock your wings
questions.why: An abrupt break-away climbing turn of 90° or more, without crossing your line of flight, means you may proceed, and an airplane answers by rocking its wings [[34:23|AIM TBL 5-6-1]]. Rocking wings ahead of you, then a slow level turn, means follow me; circling the airport with the gear down means land there [[34:23|AIM TBL 5-6-1]]. When intercepted, the code is 7700 unless ATC tells you otherwise, not 7600 [[34:22|AIM 5-6-13]]. A TFR is a type of NOTAM, and only national security TFRs are on the chart [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]], so check NOTAMs before you go.

questions.q: A mechanic opened the static line behind the panel to replace a cracked fitting and signed off the repair. The 24-month altimeter, static and encoder check was done 10 months ago. You want to fly IFR in controlled airspace tomorrow. What else is required?
options: Nothing; the 24-month check is still current
A static system test and inspection after the opening, by an authorized person such as an airframe-rated mechanic
You may check it yourself by opening the alternate static source during the runup
Only a VOR check within the last 30 days
questions.why: For IFR in controlled airspace, any opening and closing of the static system, other than using the drains and the alternate static valve, must be followed by a static system test and inspection [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]]. A certificated mechanic with an airframe rating may do the static system test [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(b)]]. The 24-month check does not cover a later opening. A leaking or partly blocked static system can look normal on the ground, then show wrong altitude, airspeed and vertical speed in a climb or descent [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. A VOR check is a separate IFR item.

questions.q: Your POH short-field takeoff chart is based on 10° of flap. To get off a short strip sooner, a coworker suggests using 25°. What is true?
options: The chart no longer applies; past about 15° flaps add a lot of drag, and the AFH says never exceed the AFM/POH flap setting for takeoff
Flap setting affects only landing distance, not takeoff
More flap means more lift, so the chart distance becomes conservative
Use 25° and add 10 percent to the chart distance
questions.why: Every chart is built on certain conditions [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]], so a different flap setting puts you outside its data. Up to 15° flaps mainly add lift; beyond 15° they bring a large increase in drag [[24:233|AFH 12-2]], which hurts acceleration and climb. The AFH is blunt: under no circumstances should the AFM/POH flap setting for takeoff be exceeded [[24:236|AFH 12-5]]. No chart note supports a 10 percent fudge for it.

questions.q: Your baseline day minimums are a 3,000 ft ceiling and 5 miles visibility. Today you are tired after a long workday, and you will fly a client's airplane with avionics you do not know. Using the RMH method, which destination TAF line for your ETA meets your adjusted minimums?
options: FM181800 27010KT 6SM -SHRA OVC038
FM181800 27010KT P6SM BKN035
FM181800 27010KT 5SM BR OVC045
FM181800 27010KT P6SM OVC045
questions.why: The RMH adds at least 500 ft to the ceiling and 1/2 mile to visibility for a special condition, such as fatigue or unfamiliar avionics, and you may make an adjustment for each one [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Two conditions: 3,000 + 2 x 500 = 4,000 ft and 5 + 2 x 1/2 = 6 miles. Only OVC045 with P6SM, which means more than 6 SM [[28:411|AWH 27-10]], meets both. BKN035 and OVC038 are below 4,000 ft, and 5SM is below 6 miles. Never lower your minimums to make a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

questions.q: You just passed your commercial ASEL checkride. You hold an instrument rating and 285 hours total. A Part 135 on-demand operator offers to make you PIC on its VFR charters right away. What is the problem?
options: None; a commercial certificate and a second-class medical are all you need
You may fly only cargo for the operator until you hold an ATP
Part 135 VFR PIC needs at least 500 hours as a pilot, including 100 hours of cross-country and 25 hours at night
Part 135 PIC needs 1,200 hours for any flight, VFR or IFR
questions.why: Commercial privileges hold only if you are qualified under the other parts that apply to the operation [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]]. For a certificate holder, VFR PIC needs at least 500 hours as a pilot, including 100 hours of cross-country time, 25 of them at night, plus an instrument rating in an airplane [[6:87|14 CFR 135.243(b)]]. The 1,200-hour minimum is for PIC under IFR [[6:87|14 CFR 135.243(c)]], not VFR. Neither rule asks for an ATP.

questions.q: Climbing on an IFR clearance through cloud at -4 °C, you notice the altimeter stuck at 6,200 ft and the VSI on zero, while the airspeed keeps decreasing with steady pitch and power. What is happening, and what do you do?
options: The pitot tube and its drain are blocked; turn on pitot heat and trust the airspeed
Ice has blocked the static ports; open the alternate static source, expect small errors, and get out of the icing
The vacuum pump failed; cover the attitude and heading indicators
The airplane is really slowing; lower the nose and keep climbing in the cloud
questions.why: Trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter at the altitude of the blockage and leaves the VSI on a continuous zero, and above that altitude the airspeed reads lower than actual [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. Confirm it by opening the alternate static source while climbing or descending; if the needles move, keep using it [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. On cabin alternate static, expect the altimeter slightly high, the airspeed high and a brief climb on the VSI [[1:205|PHAK 8-3]]. A pitot tube and drain blocked together would make the airspeed rise in a climb, like an altimeter, and the altimeter would still move [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. Ice on the airframe means an airplane not certified for icing must exit it at once [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13]].
